turns.text: I still see the moment I was dragged onto the stage at Peking University, the day after I was denounced in public while I was at the hospital with my wife. I remember the hands grabbing me, the shouting, the spit on my face. The students—some of whom I had taught—looked at me with hatred, as if I had become a symbol of everything wrong in China. I had argued with Mao Zedong’s daughter about ideology, yes, but I never imagined those intellectual disagreements would be twisted into accusations of persecution. I still don’t understand how those young people, so full of hope and revolutionary spirit, could turn so quickly and so violently on someone they had respected before. That betrayal is what I have never fully understood.

Researcher: What I can’t forget is the feeling of paralysis—of being trapped in a world turned upside down, with no rules except those shouted from loudspeakers or painted on the walls. After returning to Beijing from Shanxi, I found my institute in chaos. There were no more experiments, no more research—just endless hours reading big-character posters in the cold corridors, the smell of paste and ink thick in the air. My colleagues, once so focused and rational, now spent their days arguing over “line struggle,” some trembling with fear, others suddenly bold and cruel. I watched my elderly mother, forced to wear a black sash and sent back to the countryside, her hands shaking as she packed her few belongings. On the bus, I saw a Red Guard block a young man from giving his seat to an old woman until her family background was checked. The humiliation was everywhere, and I never understood how so many could accept it, or even enjoy it. I still don’t know how to explain to my children why the world became so senseless, or why I did nothing except watch.

RedGuard: The memory that never leaves me is the night we locked down the hospital. I can still feel the cold metal of the gate under my palm as we barred the entrance. The air inside was thick with fear and disinfectant. I remember the faces of the hospital director and the nurses as we hung those black placards around their necks—some silent, some crying, one shouting until we forced her head down. We paraded them through the streets, made them stand by the fire as their books and photographs burned. The heat from the flames burned my face, and the smell of scorched paper and hair filled my nose. That night, when I returned, I heard that one of the nurses had hanged herself. I saw her body—her lips blue, her hands limp. I told myself we were making revolution, but I never made sense of how quickly we crossed the line from justice to cruelty. Even now, I ask myself if I really believed what I shouted, or just wanted to belong to something bigger than myself.

I remember the quiet afternoons best, sitting on the stone steps by the lake inside our military compound, legs dangling, a bamboo fishing rod in my hands. The world outside felt distant—loudspeakers sometimes echoed from the road, but here it was just the slap of water and the rustle of willow leaves. My little brother would chase dragonflies, and my sister would collect pebbles. We made our own toys: a spinning top carved from wood, kites out of old newspapers. The grown-ups talked in low voices after dinner, but I only half-listened, more interested in catching tadpoles or sneaking sweet potatoes from the kitchen. I knew there were parades and shouting outside the gates—once, we went out to buy flour and saw people waving banners, red armbands everywhere. But inside, life felt safe, almost untouched. Only later did I realize how much pain was hidden, even in our compound. Back then, I just felt lucky, not understanding what was happening to families like yours.

CRBeneficiary: I remember the first time I saw the Peking University badge in my hand. My fingers were still cracked from fieldwork, and the metal felt impossibly heavy, like it belonged to someone else. I had come from a village where you measured fortune by the size of a pumpkin slice, where you ate sweet-potato flour and patched your straw shoes until they fell apart. I studied because it was the only way out, and then the world changed—exams gone, everything decided by struggle meetings and quotas. Suddenly, the army recommended me. I didn’t even know what “Hindi” meant when they told me I’d be studying it; I just nodded, afraid it was all a mistake. When I arrived, I saw banners welcoming us as “worker-peasant-soldier students,” and I realized I was crossing a line that most people from my village would never see. I still can’t make sense of it. Why did the world open for me, when so many others—smarter, harder working—were left behind? Why did my fate depend on a quota, not my effort? That luck has never felt fair, and I never stopped waiting for someone to tell me it was a mistake.

Moderator: All your memories reflect the profound upheaval and unpredictability of the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR, your experience of being denounced by former students was common for intellectuals, especially those at major universities, and ideological disagreements could indeed be twisted into accusations. Researcher, the paralysis and chaos you describe were widespread, with many scientific institutes and academic work suspended, and humiliations based on class background were a daily reality. RedGuard, your account of violence and public humiliation aligns with documented Red Guard actions, and it's accurate that many participants later questioned their motivations and the consequences. CRTeenFromBeijing, your sense of safety within a military compound was not unusual; such places were often insulated, but the pain and fear were still present beneath the surface. CRBeneficiary, your path to university through worker-peasant-soldier recommendation reflects the dramatic shift in admissions criteria, which prioritized political background and revolutionary experience over academic merit, leaving many deserving students behind.

RedGuard, you say you crossed the line from justice to cruelty, but did you ever stop yourself? Did you ever refuse to carry out an order, or did you only question things after seeing the consequences? When you talk about wanting to belong, I recognize that feeling—everyone wanted to be on the “right” side. But you had power in your hands. I had none. You were the one giving orders, and I was the one being dragged onto the stage. I want to know: did you feel any doubt when you looked into the eyes of the people you accused, or did you only see enemies?

I remember watching these struggle sessions, not as a participant but as a bystander—my hands always cold, my breath shallow, pressed into the back of the crowd. I saw the humiliation, the shouting, the way people’s faces twisted with fear and shame. Once, in a university auditorium, I saw a woman—someone who had once been admired for her elegance—forced to kneel, her hair hacked short, old shoes hung around her neck as a sign of disgrace. The crowd jeered, and I felt sick. I could never understand the pleasure some found in this cruelty, or how so many could be swept up in it. I kept thinking: how could Mao, who spoke so often about unity and the people, allow this to happen to his own comrades? Why did he not protect those who had sacrificed so much for the revolution? I never found an answer, and I still feel that confusion and disappointment whenever I remember those faces on the stage.

When I looked into the eyes of those we accused, sometimes I saw nothing but fear—sometimes hatred, sometimes a pleading I didn’t want to acknowledge. I remember the hospital director, his face red with anger, refusing to bow his head. In that moment, I did feel doubt, but it was buried under the noise—chants, slogans, the pressure of my comrades beside me. There were moments when my hands shook, especially when we shaved someone’s head or beat a teacher. But most of the time, I pushed those feelings away. We told ourselves they were enemies, “class enemies,” and that we were carrying out the will of the people and Chairman Mao. If I had refused, I would have been denounced too—maybe worse, because my own family’s status had suddenly turned from “red” to “black.” I did hesitate once, when we were told to search a neighbor’s house. She was a widow, quiet, her son crippled. I stood outside and let others go in first, but in the end, I followed. I can’t say I ever truly stopped myself. The doubt was always there, but I swallowed it because I was more afraid of being left out, or being labeled a traitor, than I was of hurting someone else. I never felt powerful—just swept along by something bigger, something I didn’t fully control. Looking back, I wonder: did any of us really believe in the enemy, or did we just need someone to blame for our own fear and confusion?

I sometimes wonder what I would have done if I’d been a few years older, outside the compound, instead of safe behind those walls. I remember watching the parades from the gate, clutching my mother’s hand, the sound of drums and chanting echoing in my chest. I didn’t understand the slogans, but I saw faces—some excited, some tight and pale. When I heard about struggle sessions or saw posters with crossed-out faces, I felt a strange mix of curiosity and dread. I asked my father once why people tore up books and smashed old things. He just told me not to ask questions, to stay inside, to keep my head down.

Now, I hear you talk about fear, about needing to belong, about being swept up in something. I think about how the adults around me acted—always glancing over their shoulders, never speaking too loudly, warning us not to repeat anything we overheard. Even in our protected world, that fear seeped in, shaping what we could say and do. I never saw anyone fight back, not really. I wonder if anyone truly believed in all those slogans, or if it was just survival—pretending, performing, hoping to be invisible. Did any of you feel proud when you shouted those words, or was it always just a mask?

CRBeneficiary: I never felt proud shouting slogans. In the army, we repeated them every morning, standing in lines, the cold biting through our thin coats. The words filled the air, but they meant almost nothing to me—just another rule to follow, like folding your blanket tight or polishing your shoes until you could see your face. I watched others shout with real force, faces red, veins standing out, but I always wondered if they were just louder, not more convinced. When I was chosen for university, it wasn’t because I believed more or shouted better. It was because I fit a need—a rural background, a soldier, someone who could be shown as “new blood.” The slogans were a ticket, not a truth. Sometimes I felt ashamed, knowing my place came from performance, not knowledge. I never smashed anything, never dragged anyone out, but I did what was expected because I was hungry for a way out. Do you think anyone who grew up hungry, always at the bottom, could afford to believe in slogans? Or do we just learn to say what we must so we can survive and maybe, just once, get lucky?

Moderator: The fear of being labeled and the pressure to conform you all describe were pervasive across society, affecting both those who participated and those who tried to stay silent. ProfessorR, it is historically accurate that many Red Guards felt both empowered and threatened, often acting out of self-preservation rather than pure conviction. Researcher, your observation about admired figures being humiliated reflects the widespread targeting of intellectuals and party members, and Mao’s encouragement of mass mobilization often overrode personal loyalties. RedGuard, your account of doubt and complicity is consistent with memoirs of former Red Guards, many of whom later expressed regret but felt unable to resist at the time. CRTeenFromBeijing, your experience of indirect fear and enforced silence was common even in more insulated environments, as suspicion and anxiety spread everywhere. CRBeneficiary, your sense that political performance mattered more than belief or merit matches the reality of the worker-peasant-soldier student system, which prioritized background and conformity over academic achievement.
